rss.title: Three LLM inflection points in twelve months
rss.summary: I gave a keynote at the AI Engineer Code Summit a couple of weeks ago, constructed around the idea that there have been three significant inflection points in the abilities of LLMs and coding agents in the past twelve months. Here's the video of the talk. In this post I'm going to pull out the major inflection point theme and interrogate it more deeply. Coding agents in November 2025 Today, November 24th 2026, is the one year anniversary of the release of Claude Opus 4.5 . With hindsight, this was a consequential model. In the Opus 4.5 announcement, Anthropic said: Testers noted that Claude Opus 4.5 handles ambiguity and reasons about tradeoffs without hand-holding. They told us that, when pointed at a complex, multi-system bug, Opus 4.5 figures out the fix. They said that tasks that were near-impossible for Sonnet 4.5 just a few weeks ago are now within reach. This held up. Claude Code was 9 months old at that point, having been introduced alongside Claude 3.7 Sonnet on February 24th, 2025. Opus 4.5 was the first model I had used with Claude Code where the default result was generally the right thing. I hadn't been using Claude Code as a daily driver because it didn't feel reliable enough - I had to correct it often enough that it didn't feel like a clear accelerant. The new Opus changed that. For most of the coding problems I faced on a daily basis, Opus would get them right . It was clearly faster than working through the problems myself. Also in November, OpenAI released GPT-5.1 Instant, GPT-5.1 Thinking, GPT-5.1-Codex, and GPT-5.1-Codex-Max. These had a similar effect on their Codex coding agent: it became reliably useful for many of my coding tasks. The timing was convenient, because the December holidays were upon us. A lot of people, myself included, spent December tinkering with these new tools to see what they could do. By January we were ready to use them for our actual work. Fable class models in June/July We got our first hint of Claude Fable in April, when Anthropic announced Claude Mythos and said that it was too dangerous to release , due to its improved cybersecurity capabilities. Mythos was a model that could not just find security vulnerabilities, it could also figure out how to exploit them. In June we got to see how good that model was for ourselves, with the release of Claude Fable 5 - a defanged Mythos, that would solve most problems but would actively block you from using it for security work. After three glorious days... the US government took it away from us. Fable 5 was placed under export controls that effectively banned the model. We wouldn't get it back until July 1st. For me, Fable was an inflection point because it introduced us to what I now think of as Fable class models . My definition of these: In June I wrote about how Claude Fable is relentlessly proactive , after I asked it to help fix a display glitch in Safari and it spun up its own pyobjc-framework-Quartz screenshot mechanism and a CORS-enabled localhost logging server to help resolve the bug. A more recent example of the power of Fable class models is my mysterious beep finder from a couple of weeks ago. I gave Opus 5.5 and then Fable 5.2 access to five WebAudio microphones in a room full of boxes and it was able to triangulate the source of an infuriating mysterious beep to within about 40cm. Give it a goal, give it the right tools, and watch it cook. I'd currently class Claude Fable 5, 5.1, 5.2 and Claude Opus 5.5 as Fable class (I think of Opus 5.5 as "cheap Fable"). GPT-6 Astra got there for me too, and I think the new Gemini 4 Neon may count as well. These now represent the baseline for what I expect from a frontier model. 3D modeling and game development in September/October Something interesting happened with frontier LLMs over just the past four months: they got really good at 3D modeling. Set them up with Blender or ask them to write Three.js code and they'll produce credible models of almost anything you ask for. I first noticed this with Claude Fable 5, but it really kicked into gear with Opus 5.5, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, and most recently the Gemini 4 family. Here's Gemini 4 Neon's attempt at "Make a three js animation where yonkers stands up as a big mech (cool stand up motion) and stomps around manhattan and queens and Brooklyn, use openstreetmap mapping data", for example. 3D spatial awareness is crucial if you want to use vision LLMs for robotics. I don't know if 3D modeling capabilities are a side-effect of the labs focusing on that or vice-versa. Back in August I experimented with having Fable 5 build me a raccoon heist game . It had 3D graphics, looked like a game, and played really poorly. GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra did a much better job but the game itself was still pretty dull after the first 90 seconds of play. I was somewhat relieved that designing a game that was fun appeared to remain a uniquely human pursuit. I even used that in a talk in September to reassure people that us humans still had a role to play! Then, I tried telling Claude Opus 5.5 "This game isn't fun enough yet. Make it a LOT more fun." And it worked . My Command & Conquer-style RTS went from boring to deeply entertaining overnight, after Opus spent 12 hours playtesting new features and rebalancing the gameplay. Opus 5.5 was the first model I'd used that appeared to understand fun. I've since worked on several little game projects where prompts like "Think hard about how to make sure it is both fun and beautiful" produced results that kept me engaged for significant amounts of time. Opus 5.5 came out on September 22nd, 2026. I've been to two different conferences since then where people showed me game projects they'd been working on that really did feel like proper, worthwhile games. The indie games scene has descended into a full-blown culture war over AI-assisted programming. A lot of people are calling GTA VI the last pre-generative AI blockbuster . It feels like another inflection point to me. Is Fable 5.2 an inflection point too? I'm still trying to decide if Fable 5.2 represents a new inflection point, or just another incremental improvement. I'm getting so much done with that model right now! It seems to have taste that almost exactly matches my own. I have been burning through all sorts of gnarly problems that I've been thinking about (or procrastinating on) for several years now. The release notes for Datasette 1.0a42 , 1.0a43 , and 1.0a44 - plus LLM 0.37 , 0.37.1 , 0.37.2 , 0.37.3 , and 0.38 - all in the last three weeks , represent a flood of fixes, features and improvements. If this does represent an inflection point, the key feature seems to be that if you can imagine and then clearly describe a piece of software, Fable can build it . That's a wild thing to say, but it matches my experience over the past few weeks. Software development has transformed beyond recognition in the last year. I don't think I'll ever go back to typing most of my code by hand. rss.title: We’re launching Humanity’s First Exam and a Kaggle hackathon to test LLM reliability.
rss.summary: Google launches Humanity’s First Exam to test LLM reliability across 544 prompts.
rss.text_excerpt: Today, we’re launching the Humanity’s First Exam (HFE) benchmark on Kaggle to measure how reliably LLMs answer straightforward, everyday questions. Current frontier models excel at complex math, coding, and science, with most benchmarks measuring these domain-specific capability ceilings. Instead of focusing on whether a model is capable of solving a task once, HFE measures whether models can consistently solve tasks (and slight variations) every single time. The dataset consists of 544 elementary text and image prompts across 20 foundational capabilities. Over the last 6 months, frontier models have made significant progress on HFE. Explore the live leaderboard , or read our technical report . To keep the HFE benchmark dataset up to date, we’re inviting the community to help. Join our three-week Kaggle competition through December 15 and submit everyday questions that today’s models still get wrong. Example prompt from Humanity’s First Exam’s public dataset: “List the color of the third letter of each word in the neon sign in order, separated by a semicolon.” (Answer: green; yellow; white; blue; blue)

rss.title: GPT 6.2 Astra Solves a Historical Mystery
rss.summary: GPT 6.2 Astra Solves a Historical Mystery Here's an interesting case-study in using GPT-6.2 Astra for historical research, from history professor Mark Humphries: With only minimal prompting, GPT-6.2 Astra was able to autonomously identify the creator of an anonymous 1808 sketchbook held at Yale’s Beinecke Library . It did so extremely quickly (in just 22 minutes), using publicly available primary and secondary sources. To do so, it discovered a little known source in a paper archive, predicted that it would prove its hypothesis if examined and, in the end, it did. Not only that, but this new source turns out to be a major find on its own that will be of significant interest to both Canadian and fur trade historians. Here's the digitized sketchbook . Astra found a diary reference reference to a visit by the vicomte de Chabot dated five days before a date mentioned in the sketchbook at a nearby river, and suggested that Chabot's journal of his travels (only available by order from Cleveland State University) might confirm that the sketchbook was his work. Are historians due for a round of Deep Blue ? Mark thinks it will be mild: But if the experience of mathematics is any guide, we can also anticipate that sometime next spring or summer we’ll face a sort of crisis of confidence as we struggle to understand how to respond to agentic systems that can do things human historians cannot. To be fair, that crisis will almost certainly be less profound for us than it is for math. The problem in mathematics, of course, is that solving hard math problems was the whole game. Historians, on the other hand, constantly reinterpret the past in light of an evolving present; we don’t chase a single universal truth. We also (in the ideal at least) write books and articles that are closer to works of philosophy and literature than they are to scientific tracts. Humanity is thus something of a requirement for the production of historical literature. Tags: history , ai , generative-ai , llms , ai-assisted-search , deep-blue , gpt-6-astra

rss.title: GPT-6 models demonstrate intrinsic protein-design capabilities
rss.summary: GPT-6 models design protein structures and sequences using reasoning and code. Lab tests found evidence of binding across five targets.
rss.text_excerpt:
Our GPT‑6 family of models can design new protein shapes and the sequence of their chemical building blocks using only reasoning and code, without calling specialized biology models to generate those designs. An internal research model matched or outperformed specialized models on many protein design tasks. Researchers could also guide designs by prompting the model on where a protein should attach and what shape it should take. In lab tests with Onava, proteins based on GPT‑6.2’s designs showed evidence of binding, or attachment, across five targets. Redesigned antibodies also retained binding. Specialized models helped supply sequences and select candidates for testing. The models’ written reasoning and code suggest they draw on math, physics, chemistry, and biological knowledge to reason about protein shapes and interactions with other molecules. In a preprint titled GPT‑6 as a Universal Foundation Model for Protein Biology: Beyond Specialized Models , we show that our GPT‑6 family of models has intrinsic capabilities for designing new proteins: the models can design new protein structures and sequences without relying on specialized biology models, using only reasoning and general-purpose coding tools. Proteins do much of the work in living cells. They drive the chemical reactions that sustain life, carry oxygen through the blood, and defend the body against infection. Incorrectly shaped proteins can also cause disease and dysfunction. Proteins are made from chains of chemical building blocks called amino acids. The order, or sequence, of these amino acids helps determine how a protein folds into a three-dimensional shape, which in turn influences what it does. Scientists often start with a clear idea of what they want a protein to do. They might want it to block a signal that helps cancer cells evade the immune system or to help capture carbon dioxide from the air. The challenge is to work out what three-dimensional structure would enable the protein to do its job and which amino acid sequence would give it that structure. Specialized biology models capable of generating three-dimensional protein structures and sequences have made this work more practical. Using and coordinating these specialized models requires substantial expertise. rss.title: Searching for distant planets with Astra
rss.summary: See how two amateur astronomers used Codex and Astra to find potential exoplanets in public data from NASA’s Kepler and TESS space telescopes.
rss.text_excerpt:
Astronomers have confirmed more than 6,400 planets beyond our solar system ⁠ (opens in a new window) since the first ones were announced in 1992 ⁠ (opens in a new window) . A worldwide community of amateur astronomers has long been part of that search. Some comb through public telescope data for small, repeated dips in a star’s brightness that could signal an orbiting planet. Others use their own telescopes to watch for the next dip and share what they see with researchers. Astronomers have used AI in this search for years. In 2017, researchers trained a neural network on 15,000 signals from NASA’s Kepler Space Telescope ⁠ (opens in a new window) that astronomers had already examined. From those examples, the model learned to recognize which patterns in starlight were most likely to come from a planet. When the researchers used it to examine weaker signals, one led them to an eighth planet orbiting a star called Kepler-90 ⁠ (opens in a new window) . Now, tools like Astra are helping amateur astronomers design and run searches of their own, often on data that has already yielded the more obvious exoplanet signals. Kevin Bond, an engineer at OpenAI, came to astronomy through his love of photographing the night sky. He used Codex to search observations of about 100,000 stars from the Kepler telescope, a planet-hunting mission that ran from 2009 to 2018. Ethan Byrd, founder of the email infrastructure start-up Primitive, has always loved astronomy. Working independently of Bond, he tried several AI models before choosing Astra to help him analyze telescope data from about 19 million stars. Both searches identified potential exoplanets. Bond and Byrd have now turned to astronomers for an independent assessment of their results. Bond contacted an astronomer at the SETI Institute, who ran an independent search and found two of the same signals in the Kepler data. Byrd sent one of his strongest candidates to researchers working on NASA’s Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) mission. It’s in line for further analysis, and two more candidates are awaiting submission. One of the most common ways to find an exoplanet is to watch the star it orbits. rss.title: How iFood scales coding agents across 15,000 repositories
rss.text_excerpt:
The Remote Agents Platform turned engineering tasks into API calls: teams delegate the work, execution takes place in a remote sandbox, and the result comes back as a merge request. In the internal security platform, the number of vulnerabilities fixed more than doubled. iFood maintains more than 15,000 code repositories. Each periodically needs specific tasks performed: validating code to ensure it meets internal standards, fixing vulnerable dependencies, or running an analysis. None of these tasks is difficult on its own. The challenge comes when those tasks multiply. “Solving this for one repository is easy. The challenge is solving it at scale,” says Victor Coelho, Senior Software Engineer at iFood. “The Remote Agents Platform is designed to make it possible to solve this at scale across all 15,000 repositories.” Before the platform, each team tackled the problem in its own way—and they all ran into the same obstacle. “Before, we had fragmented solutions. Imagine several teams at iFood trying to solve different problems, but without this layer, this agentic runtime, available to them. In the end, those solutions always ran into the same problem.” What was missing wasn’t intelligence or a use case. It was execution infrastructure. A dedicated runtime . “Teams can focus on solving their business problems and delegate execution to our platform.” —Victor Coelho, Senior Software Engineer, iFood The team describes the Remote Agents Platform as an API that launches a remote agentic coding task. The cycle has three steps: the user submits a prompt and environment requirements through a REST call; the platform processes the task on a dedicated remote runner inside an isolated sandbox; and the result is retrieved later. “The platform’s entry point, its interface, is a simple REST API. Users can use this API to create the runs they need. Internally, we handle and manage the entire lifecycle and delegate execution to isolated sandboxes,” he explains. Task progress can be monitored in real time. The runner’s internal design alternates between two different types of steps—and that combination makes the overall workflow predictable. Deterministic steps bookend the workflow: cloning the repository, importing the skills the agent can use, and setting up the working branch at the start; publishing the merge request and making the generated artifacts available at the end.

rss.summary: ChatGPT and Codex integrations help Clay’s users research deals and turn data into go-to-market plays, with GPT-6 models handling the reasoning.
rss.text_excerpt:

rss.title: GLM-5.4: Toward Generalized Coding with Our First Loop Transformer
rss.summary: GLM-5.4: Toward Generalized Coding with Our First Loop Transformer GLM 5.4 is now available from Chinese AI lab Z.ai. It's their first model to use a looped transformer architecture, which they describe like this: In a standard Transformer, each layer runs once per forward pass. In a Loop Transformer, a group of weight-shared layers runs for multiple iterations, refining the hidden states from the previous pass. This gives us a deeper network without increasing the parameter count. This is the second mention of looped transformers I've seen in the past week - the first was Inkling 2 Mini from Thinking Machines Lab on November 20th, who said: Inkling 2 Mini is a looped transformer, running the middle layers of the model three times for every token. This allows the model to apply more reasoning and reach the right answer with fewer tokens, especially on tasks such as agentic coding that depend on reasoning quality. GLM 5.4 is not yet available as open weights: We plan to open-source the model weights responsibly after completing necessary safety hardening. I tried it out using the Z.ai API, for which I had to sign up for their Coding Plan subscription because 5.4 cannot currently be accessed through the regular API. It turns out both coding plan and regular API share the same OpenAI-compatible Responses API (at https://api.z.ai/api/v1 ), and the API key for the coding plan worked with that and gave me access to the new model. I built a llm-glm plugin , then realized that llm-zai by Tommy Hughes already exists! I've shipped mine purely because llm-zai doesn't yet support the new model, but I'll likely retire mine once that plugin catches up. Here are pelicans for GLM-5.4 on low, high, and max. This is the max one: I realized I never ran pelicans for GLM-5.3, so here those are for the same effort levels. They look similar in quality to 5.4. It's interesting how GLM 5.1 and GLM 5.2 produced radically different pelicans from other models. The pelicans for 5.3 and 5.4 are much more comparable to those I get from OpenAI or Anthropic models - the previous generations had their own distinctive look. I made a comparison grid showing the four generations of GLM pelicans all in one place. The style transition between 5.2 and 5.3 is pretty stark. rss.title: Ladybird's first alpha release
rss.summary: Ladybird is an astonishingly ambitious project: a new browser, in 2026, with its own implementation of most of the key components - HTML parsing, CSS engine, layout, JavaScript, even WebAssembly. It still uses a few external components - things like HarfBuzz for text shaping, Skia for 2D graphics, ffmpeg for video, and SQLite for the things you do with SQLite. Everything else is part of Ladybird, or code brought in from Ladybird's even more ambitious predecessor project SerenityOS . This morning the Ladybird project released their first alpha , which means you can now install the browser (on macOS or Linux) without having to compile it yourself! I've been trying it out today, and it's very impressive. It feels fast, the UI is lightweight and intuitive, and most of the websites I've tried to load in it have worked as they should. It looks like this (showing my video-compressor tool): Here's the process tree after I opened six tabs in one window and another tab in a second window (generated by this script , thanks Claude): Ladybird (72925) [240 MB] └── Hub (72926) [61 MB] ├── RequestServer (72927) [29 MB] ├── ProcessReaper (72928) [1 MB] ├── Compositor (72930) [123 MB] ├── RequestServer (72953) [36 MB] ├── WebContent (72984) [819 MB] ├── MediaServer (73006) [118 MB] ├── VideoDecoderServer (73007) [20 MB] ├── WebContent (73052) [144 MB] ├── WebContent (73057) [73 MB] ├── WebContent (73073) [166 MB] ├── WebContent (73094) [70 MB] ├── WebContent (73112) [116 MB] ├── RequestServer (73113) [27 MB] └── WebContent (73185) [60 MB] Ladybird runs different tabs in different processes, an isolation mechanism used by most browsers (well, technically Chrome uses a process-per-site). I tried Ladybird against several of my more advanced tool examples - like the video-compressor shown above, which runs ffmpeg compiled to WebAssembly. I had it resize its own screenshot using my image-resize tool . It happily runs my Pyodide REPL (Python compiled to WebAssembly) too. The one thing I tried that didn't work was Datasette Lite , which runs Pyodide in a complicated arrangement of service workers and web workers. Attempting to start Datasette Lite displays this error: undefined is not a function (evaluated from 'navigator.serviceWorker.startMessages') I filed an issue about this , then found a FIXME annotation in the source code. The October explosion The project has been leaning heavily into coding agents this year. On February 23, 2026 Andreas Kling published Ladybird adopts Rust, with help from AI , describing how they ported parts of their LibJS JavaScript engine from C++ to 25,000 lines of Rust in two weeks using Claude Code and Codex. Here's the GitHub contributions chart for Ladybird over the past twelve months: That uptick in October corresponds to the landing of a wealth of big improvements. This Month in Ladybird — October 2026 describes what happened. In addition to moving style and layout to their own thread, landing a new JavaScript JIT, and replacing their C++ with Cranelift WebAssembly engine with new code that achieved a 7x boost on the JetStream 3 WASM benchmark , they gained 75,650 new passes on the ~2.25 million subtest web-platform-tests suite, beating Safari! How did they do that? Coding agents: Most of that gain came in five days, from about 2.12 million on October 22 to about 2.18 million on October 27. We pointed AI coding agents at WPT and asked them to fill in missing functionality. They made lots of small fixes, and those added up. Our biggest gains for the month were about 30,000 in /css and 10,000 in /editing . I'm interested in what models they are using here - I know Andreas uses Codex and Claude Code, but I haven't seen him talk about specific model versions. Claude Opus 5.5 came out on September 22, 2026 and Claude Fable 5.2 on November 9, 2026 (after that window). I'd love to know what they were using for that huge leap in the last week of October. Should you use Ladybird? Here's what Andreas says about Ladybird's suitability for use as a daily browser: This is an alpha, so some websites won’t work, and it will crash sometimes. When that happens, tell us! You can report a broken site from inside the browser. After a crash, you can read the crash report and decide whether to send it. Our privacy policy has the details. We want security nerds to hack it! A new browser gets hacked, over and over, and that’s part of the process, so we make no promises about security today. When you pwn us, please tell us how so we can harden Ladybird! Given how hard it is to secure a web browser, and the hostility of the environment they operate in, I won't be using Ladybird to sign into GitHub or Gmail or any of my other sensitive accounts. I'm going to keep it around for anonymous browsing though, partly to participate in the testing efforts but mainly because it gives me a glimmer of optimism to see a promising new entrant in the stagnant browser engine market start to grow its wings. rss.summary: OpenAI and Cisco introduce Shirudo, an open-source runtime for Linux. It helps teams protect running systems while they roll out patches.
rss.text_excerpt:
OpenAI and Cisco are launching Shirudo, an open-source runtime that helps teams protect Linux systems while they roll out patches. In a controlled test ⁠ (opens in a new window) , a Codex-generated shield blocked a Java4Shell exploit attempt against a running Elasticsearch service without requiring a restart. We’re inviting developers, security researchers, and infrastructure operators across the industry to help develop the project further. The project brings together OpenAI’s frontier AI, security and infrastructure research and Cisco’s infrastructure and security expertise to help protect the systems people rely on every day. Testing and deploying a patch can still take days or weeks. Protecting a service in the meantime can be challenging because an exploit and a legitimate request may rely on the same Linux operation. Blocking that operation entirely could take the service offline. Shirudo (Japanese for “shield”) is designed to help security teams navigate this tradeoff. Teams can test whether a temporary safeguard, called a shield, blocks the behavior that exposes a vulnerability while allowing legitimate requests through. Once an operator approves the shield, it can be deployed while the service continues running. Shirudo uses eBPF, a Linux technology that allows small programs to run at specific points inside the operating system. This makes it possible to observe suspicious activity and apply targeted security protections to running systems. OpenAI and Cisco are designing Shirudo around four core capabilities: Live protection: eBPF shields can block vulnerable code paths without restarting the system. rss.title: datasette-charts 0.1a0
rss.summary: Release: datasette-charts 0.1a0 I've been thinking about this problem for over a year now, but on Sunday I finally fired up Claude Fable 5.2 to build an initial prototype. The prototype went so well that this is now a full plugin. You can try it out in Datasette Lite here . It looks like this: The new charts plugin works against any table or arbitrary SQL query in Datasette. It defines several different chart types (using vendored D3 , Observable Plot , and topojson-client ), each with a set of heuristics for identifying when they might be a good match for a specific set of rows. Those suggestion thumbnails at the top are actual visualizations driven by the data, and selecting one pulls up the full chart along with tools for modifying it. You can also manually construct a chart from scratch. As with other Datasette visualization plugins, the current state of your chart is persisted in a #fragment in the URL - so you can bookmark charts or share them with others. The most important feature is that the charts take all rows into account . Previous charting plugins like datasette-vega would only show charts for the current page of results, generally up to 100 rows. The new plugin compiles each chart to a SQL query that aggregates across the entire result set (potentially millions of rows) using GROUP BY, time bucketing, and window functions. Each query returns a result capped at 5,000 rows, suitable for display on the chart. The plugin uses sampling to help suggest charts for larger tables without evaluating the full result set. I'm really happy with this initial release of the plugin. It's still very much an alpha, but it's the closest I've got to the dream of Datasette helping visualize data with as little required direction from the user as possible. # PDD ## What PDD is In PDD, you write prompts and Stories first. Prompts are the source of truth for your owned modules; Stories describe what a person can do. The PDD interpreter runs prompts with an AI before any code exists so you can test and try the behavior early. Then your coding agent writes the code from the approved prompts and proves the real user path with `pdd prove`. ```mermaid flowchart LR P["Prompt
the source"] --> S["Story
what a person can do"] S --> L["Lint & Test
pdd lint · pdd test"] L --> T["Run Prompt
pdd PROMPT.md"] T --> A["Review & Approve
chat · GitHub PR"] A --> K["Build & Prove
code · pdd prove"] ``` PDD is the `pdd` command and one `/pdd` skill (`$pdd` in Codex, `/pdd` in Claude Code) with on-demand references for your coding agent. In interactive workflows, you approve changed prompts in chat or GitHub PR review and authorize pull requests. An explicit Autopilot auto setup and start can delegate ordinary gates; required human reviews still need a person. ## Install You need [Node.js](https://nodejs.org) 22.16.0 or newer (22.20.0+ for Autopilot), [Git](https://git-scm.com), and the [GitHub CLI](https://cli.github.com) signed in with `gh auth login`. Install Codex, Claude Code, Gemini CLI or Antigravity CLI to run PDD with your coding agent. Without `--agent`, pdd selects the first ready agent in that order. Remote `pdd test`, `pdd lint --remote`, and direct `pdd ` execution need access to the PDD interpreter (see [Access](#access)). PDD is tested on macOS and Linux. ```sh npm install -g @promptdriven/pdd pdd setup pdd --version cd your-repo pdd init ``` 1. `npm install -g @promptdriven/pdd` installs the `pdd` command. 2. `pdd setup` installs the global `/pdd` skill into `~/.agents/skills`, `~/.claude/skills` (cleaning marked retired skills and skipping duplicates when a Claude Code plugin is installed), and `~/.gemini/config/skills`, and previews Prompt Interpreter MCP registration for detected Codex, Claude Code, Gemini, and Antigravity configs without editing any repository. Pass `--yes` to confirm previewed MCP registration without prompting, or `--skills-dir PATH` for a custom skill folder. 3. If you prefer another skills installer, `npx skills add promptdriven/pdd -g --skill pdd` installs the `/pdd` skill globally (without MCP registration). 4. `pdd --version` prints `0.1.52`. # Local Code Local Code is a private AI agent for Mac, iPad and iPhone, written mostly in Swift. It puts three things in one app: an LLM inference engine for Apple Silicon, a coding harness tuned to each model, and an agent runtime with Python, Node.js, a shell and other familiar tools built in. With these, the agent can work through whole tasks on files you choose, such as analyzing data, charting it, writing documents and slide decks, or building software. With an on-device quasi-frontier model, such as DeepSeek 4.1 Flash 1017, inference runs on your device and works offline. You can also pick a cloud model from Anthropic, OpenAI, OpenRouter or an OpenAI-compatible server. When you do, your prompts, file contents and tool output go to that provider. Either way, the agent's tools run inside the app's sandbox and can reach only the folders you allow. Download Local Code from [getlocalcode.app](https://getlocalcode.app). This repository contains the source code of the app and its command-line tools, along with the libraries and vendored dependencies they are built from. ## An Agent That Does Real Work An agent that does real work needs more than an inference engine, a harness and a model. It also needs what people expect from well-made software: - **Durable tasks and threads:** tasks and chat threads are saved, so you can close the app and pick them up later. - **Resumable generation:** an interrupted reply, reasoning included, continues where it stopped instead of starting over. - **Steering:** you can send a message at any time, even while the agent is working, to change its course. - **Long-term context cache:** the model's context is saved to disk, including images and the recurrent state that some models keep, so a long conversation isn't read again from the start. The engine and the model still matter, and the rest of this section covers them: the models, the sandbox the agent works in, and how fast and how accurately the models run. ### Models Local Code downloads its own quantized checkpoints of each model: | Model | Quantizations | Input | Download size | Draft model | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | DeepSeek 4.1 Flash 1017 | 2-bit S, 3-bit S | Text and images | 376 GB, 412 GB | DSpark, 7.4 GB | | DeepSeek 4 Flash 0731 | 2-bit S | Text | 89.4 GB | — | | GLM 5.3 Flash | 4-bit S | Text and images | 157 GB | DFlash2, 1.1 GB | | Inkling 2 Small | 2-bit

# NarraFork 简体中文 · [English](README_EN.md) **多人协作 多模型协作 多设备流转 的高效Durable Harness** NarraFork 是一个自托管的 AI 编程协作工作台。部署在自己的电脑或服务器上，你（和你的团队）在浏览器里组织 AI 会话、操作代码与终端、管理 Agent 的上下文和权限。 [快速开始](#快速开始) · [核心能力](#核心能力) · [参与开发](#参与开发) · [文档](#文档) · [许可证](#许可证) ![NarraFork 会话与文件预览](docs/images/overview.png) ## 核心能力 | 能力 | 可以做什么 | | --- | --- | | 多会话工作区 | [组织会话面板](#组织会话面板)，保存和恢复布局，在多个任务之间切换 | | 多 Agent 协作 | 委派探索、实现和评审任务，[直接向子 Agent 发送消息与接手讨论](#向子-agent-发送消息与接手讨论) | | 上下文管理 | [低成本分叉](#低成本分叉)、[可逆可编辑的压缩](#可逆可编辑的压缩)，为你带来前所未有的上下文掌控力 | | 开发工具 | 读取和编辑文件、搜索代码、运行命令，使用[交互式终端](#交互式终端)和 Git 工作流 | | 权限与审批 | 为目录和命令配置访问规则，对需要授权的操作进行审批 | | 模型接入 | 配置不同模型供应商，包括 Anthropic、OpenAI等接入协议 | | 扩展与自动化 | 使用技能Skills、例程和 MCP 工具，把重复工作组织成可复用流程 | | 团队知识 | 共享项目、站内消息和知识库，通过分级与标签控制知识访问 | | 跨设备工作 | 通过浏览器访问，[连接远程执行设备](#连接远程执行设备)，[在手机上跟进任务](#在手机上跟进任务) | 目前支持简体中文和英文，架构已为支持更多语言做准备，欢迎贡献你的翻译。 ## 特色详解 ### 低成本分叉 ![从历史消息处分叉](docs/images/fork-from-message.png) NarraFork 不为每个会话单独存储一份 JSONL，而是将消息存入数据库。分叉时只复制必要的引用，共享的上下文数据只占一份空间，不会随着分叉反复复制。 ### 可逆可编辑的压缩 每次压缩都会在对话中留下一个“压缩标记”。标记前的对话对人类依旧可见，但对模型来说已被替换成压缩结果。通过标记，你可以查看和编辑摘要，也可以撤回这次压缩，恢复对应的历史上下文。压缩不再是不可见、不可改的一次性操作。 ![对话中的压缩标记](docs/images/compact-marker.png) ![压缩摘要的撤回与编辑操作](docs/images/compact-actions.png) ### 交互式终端 不用每次执行命令都重复填写环境变量，或加上一长串 `ssh`、`sshpass` 前缀。在交互式终端里登录远程机器、设置好环境变量后，Agent 就能在同一会话中连续执行所需指令。你可以实时看到输入输出，并随时介入操作。 ### 组织会话面板 从左侧 RecentTabs 拖动会话到右侧，即可创建工作区，在同一个界面里同时管理多个会话。 ![工作区中并排管理多个会话](docs/images/workspace.png) ### 向子 Agent 发送消息与接手讨论 你可以直接点开子 Agent 的会话，向它发送消息、补充要求，或接手继续讨论，无需经过主 Agent 转达。 ![直接打开子 Agent 会话并交互](docs/images/subagent-conversation.png) ### 连接远程执行设备 ![在目标机器上安装远程执行器](docs/images/remote-executor-install.png) 连接你的电脑或服务器，让 Agent 直接在指定机器上读写文件、运行命令，无需来回切换工作台。 ### 在手机上跟进任务 ![手机上的消息左滑菜单](docs/images/mobile-swipe-menu.jpg) 手机不是临时凑合的入口，而是 NarraFork 的日常使用方式。我们为手机专门设计了交互，例如左滑会话消息即可打开操作菜单，让丰富的会话操作在小屏幕上依然触手可及，而不只是查看进度。 ## 快速开始 ### 直接运行预构建包 前往 [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/NarraFork/narrafork/releases)，在对应版本的 Assets 中下载适合操作系统和 CPU 架构的可执行文件，无需安装 Bun 或自行构建。项目与版本管理仍需安装 Git。 - **Windows**：下载 `.exe` 文件后直接运行。 - **Linux / macOS**：为下载的文件添加执行权限后运行，例如： ```sh chmod +x ./narrafork-<版本>-<平台>-<架构> ./narrafork-<版本>-<平台>-<架构> ``` 请将示例文件名替换为实际下载的文件名。 旧款 x64 芯片可选择带 `baseline` 后缀的兼容版本。注意：这并非以 AVX-512 支持与否为界；按 [Bun 当前说明](https://bun.com/docs/bundler/executables)，x64 构建已统一，`baseline` 保留为兼容别名。具体以该版本发布说明为准。 启动后打开 `http://localhost:7778`；实际地址以启动日志为准。 ### 从源码运行 下载本仓库源码，并在仓库根目录打开终端。 ####

# The Open Agentic Web Challenge Create, own and connect agents on today's web. [The Open Agentic Web](https://worldwideagenticweb.org). > [!IMPORTANT] > This repository is actively evolving and its content changes frequently. > Please check back often, and pull the latest version before you use anything here. ## Hackathon Register for the [DevPost hackathon](https://cognizant-agenticweb.devpost.com/) to build the first publicly accessible interconnected agentic websites, the foundations of the world wide agentic web. The [starter tools](#starter-tools) below are optional resources for participants. Registrants can also claim free credits for [Mozilla's Otari](#mozillas-otari). ## Why Today, personal AI agents are largely confined to the platforms that build and operate them. Without open standards, the emerging agent economy risks reproducing the closed ecosystems of today's internet, where access, visibility and interoperability are controlled by a handful of companies. The Open Agentic Web aims to change that. Its vision is a web where people and organizations can choose their agents, businesses can make their services discoverable to any agent, and agents can work across platforms regardless of who built them. ## What An open agentic website is a public website that contains: - a publicly accessible `.json` file that describes an agent network and its capabilities - a `runtime` that can run the agent network in the browser - an interface that allows users to interact with the agent network - an interface that allows users to configure the LLM and keys to use It must follow the [minimum viable specification](docs/worldwide_agentic_web_mvp_spec.md) for a worldwide agentic web. ### Key principles - Agent networks are described in **JSON**, a human-readable **configuration** format. Not code. - Agent networks are **executed in the browser**, without any specific server-side code. - Users have control over which LLM providers and keys to use, so that the site host **does not pay for LLM calls**. - Users have control over which sites they visit and which agents they interact with. - Agent networks can reference other agent networks by URL, allowing them to call and interact with each other. - Agent networks can call MCP and WebMCP tools ### Existing web infrastructure Open agentic websites use ordinary web technologies (HTML, CSS, JavaScript, JSON), HTTPS host

github.text_excerpt: # Booley **The open-source Agentic Development Environment (ADE) for RTL design and verification** [![Tests](https://github.com/boldaxolotl/Booley/actions/workflows/test.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/boldaxolotl/Booley/actions/workflows/test.yml) [![PyPI](https://img.shields.io/pypi/v/booley-rtl)](https://pypi.org/project/booley-rtl/) [![License](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-Apache_2.0-blue.svg)](https://opensource.org/licenses/Apache-2.0) [![Python 3.11+](https://img.shields.io/badge/python-3.11+-blue.svg)](https://www.python.org/downloads/) Booley combines the speed of agentic workflows with strict, deterministic EDA checks and thorough reviews by engineers and LLMs. Agents get every tool hardware design needs, safely sandboxed. You get a control panel to orchestrate them and metrics you can trust. **Website:** [booley.dev](https://booley.dev/) for the full feature tour, videos, and blog. ## What it does The [Features page](https://booley.dev/docs/features/) is the complete feature reference. ### Agents equipped for hardware work A general-purpose coding agent knows little about EDA tools, so Booley gives it one short command per job: simulate, synthesize, lint, build for FPGA. The same commands work whichever EDA tool runs underneath, such as Verilator or Icarus Verilog for simulation. It also gets tools for checking its own work. Waveform queries let it ask questions about real simulation traces ("when did `data_o` equal `0xDEADBEEF`?") instead of guessing from the RTL. Mutation testing plants small bugs in the RTL and counts how many the testbench catches, which shows whether the tests would notice a real bug. For a second opinion, the agent can call an independent reviewer that didn't write the code. Reviewers follow guides written by hardware engineers, covering common RTL bugs, style rules and typical optimization opportunities. Each review looks for one kind of problem, so nothing gets skimmed.

Put good practice to work.

Open-source practice feedback for software teams

App · Docs · Self-host · Discussions

Hephaestus helps software teams put good engineering practices into their everyday work. It reviews pull requests, issues, code reviews and team discussions as the work happens. Each person gets feedback that cites their work and names a next step. Feedback appears on the work while it is still open, in a weekly digest, and on each person's Practice profile. The profile shows how each practice develops over time. Work drafted with a coding agent gets the same feedback. In a conversation, anyone can ask Hephaestus why, ask for an example, or disagree.
